components.text: Whether religious claims merely assert settled revelation or can instead be compared by their explanatory performance.
Whether the historical origin or development of religion itself establishes that the God hypothesis is false or harmful.
Whether the God hypothesis rationally explains otherwise puzzling facts better than rival accounts.
Whether a belief's natural historical development determines its present truth or explanatory merit.
Whether natural evolutionary history supplies an adequate explanation of life's origin without purposeful intelligence.
Whether explaining transitions among living forms also explains the first reproductive cell.
Whether natural history adequately explains life's origin without purposeful or intelligent causation.
Whether evolutionary transitions among organisms answer the distinct question of the first reproductive cell.
Whether cosmic history without purposeful design adequately explains the universe's life-permitting physical conditions.
Whether life-permitting cosmic conditions call for an explanation compatible with purposeful design.
Whether natural cosmic history alone explains why physical constants permit life.
Whether revelation's asserted moral answers improperly displace open ethical reasoning.
Whether morality requires accepting the geographically narrow religious account criticized by Hitchens.
Whether revelation improperly substitutes settled divine answers for open moral inquiry.
Whether human beings possess a source of ethics and morality independent of religious belief.
Whether God functions as a genuinely testable explanatory hypothesis rather than an explanation insulated from possible defeat.
Whether religious popularity or prevalence supplies evidence that religious claims are true.
Whether the proposed God explanation can face a specified observation that would count against it.
Whether religious popularity or prevalence provides evidence that the associated beliefs are true.
Whether naturalistic mechanisms adequately explain altruism toward unrelated strangers who cannot reciprocate.
Whether widespread religious experience is better explained by a real divine object.
Whether human moral dilemmas and responsibility require a supernatural explanation rather than human deliberation.
Whether religion uniquely supplies answers to persistent human ethical and existential questions.
Whether religious claims ever expose themselves to factual confirmation or failure and therefore escape blanket unfalsifiability.
Whether revelation necessarily supplies claims insulated from continuing evidential inquiry.
Whether any religious claim exposes itself to factual confirmation or failure.
Whether religious assertions are categorically insulated from evidential inquiry.
Whether humans can address persistent moral and political dilemmas without supernatural dependence.
Whether cosmic history makes geographically narrow revelation implausible as a basis for salvation or morality.
Whether secular inquiry supplies answers about life's purpose, destiny, and death.
Whether religion may legitimately address questions beyond scientific mechanism.
Whether atrocities and religiously framed violence should be causally attributed to God or to voluntary human agency.
Whether evidence of suffering or human wrongdoing defeats an independent inference from apparent design.
Whether voluntarily committed human atrocities should be attributed to God or defeat an independent design inference.
Whether historical suffering and waste logically bear on the separate inference from apparent design.
Whether locating agency in human perpetrators removes the causal and legitimating role of religious or messianic absolutism.
Whether claimed factual corroboration makes authoritative religious certainty epistemically safe.
Whether harmful conduct should be understood solely as individual free choice rather than as enabled by absolutist authority.
Whether certainty and supreme authority are epistemically safer than open-ended doubt.
Whether the historical harms cited should be attributed specifically to religion rather than conquest or broader messianic absolutism.
Whether contemporary actors' divine warrants causally intensify the particular conflicts and violence identified.
Whether historical conquest and mass killing are properly attributed to religion rather than secular utopian coercion.
Whether religious motivation is the governing cause of the cited patterns of political violence.
Whether apparent life-permitting order is better understood as purposeful direction or as a setting for contingent natural history.
Whether the origin of the first reproductive cell is adequately explained by the evolutionary branching described.
Whether contingent, branching natural history supports a purposeful design inference.
Whether evolutionary history supplies a naturalistic alternative to intelligent causation.
Whether religious judgment supplies a credible and desirable source of meaning where science leaves existential questions open.
Whether supernatural judgment supplies meaning or a legitimate purpose absent from secular life.
Whether practical religious commitment is epistemically improved by strategic profession of belief.
Whether aid to strangers can be intelligible and motivating without supernatural judgment or a distinct divine explanation.
Whether finite secular life can supply meaningful practical commitments despite science's limits.
Whether secular people can aid strangers without supernatural judgment or command.
Whether finite secular practices can be experienced as meaningful and mutually beneficial.
Whether religion uniquely or distinctively supplies purpose and transcendence beyond scientific mechanism.
Whether experiences labeled religious require a real divine object rather than secular experiential counterparts.
Whether nonreligious life can sustain meaning, transcendence, fellowship, and emotional depth.
Whether experiences associated with religion uniquely indicate a religious or divine source.
